articles.title: CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Rallied While AI Stocks Sank. Wall Street Is Pricing a Different AI Trade
articles.summary: The September 14 AI selloff produced an odd winner: cybersecurity. As chip stocks fell after frontier AI leaders called for slower development, CrowdStrike H...
articles.body:
The September 14 AI selloff produced an odd winner: cybersecurity. As chip stocks fell after frontier AI leaders called for slower development, CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWD ) and Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (NASDAQ: PANW ) both traded higher as investors also digested fresh concern about AI-enabled cyber risk and the Revolut breach.

The move suggests Wall Street may be separating the cost of building smarter models from the cost of securing systems that already exist.

Slower frontier progress can still mean more attack surface

CrowdStrike's latest quarter gives the optimistic reading substance. Revenue reached $1.47 billion, annual recurring revenue rose 25% to $5.84 billion, and record net new ARR reached $332.8 million. CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWD) can sell security into endpoints, cloud workloads, identities and AI agents regardless of whether the next frontier model arrives a few months later.

Valuation and commoditization pull the other way. If third-party foundation models supply more of the reasoning inside security products, competing vendors can license similar intelligence. CrowdStrike still has to prove that AI increases its pricing power rather than simply raising everyone else's product quality.

Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (NASDAQ:PANW) has a broader platform strategy and is buying capabilities around agentic workflows. That breadth can make it easier for large customers to consolidate security spending. The downside is integration. Acquisitions increase debt, shares outstanding and execution complexity, while management expects some next-generation security growth to decelerate after recent acquisition-assisted comparisons.

Hedge funds increased both positions before today's rotation

Insider Monkey's database showed CrowdStrike ownership rising to 89 hedge funds in Q2 2026 from 79 in Q1. D. E. Shaw held 8,533,204 common shares after increasing its position 18%. Palo Alto also reached 89 holders, up from 87, while Fisher Asset Management increased its position 2,143% to roughly 5.8 million shares. The filings predate the September 14 price action.

CrowdStrike had 24,353,332 shares sold short on August 31, equal to 2.42% of float, with 2.16 days to cover.

The rally does not mean cybersecurity is insulated from an AI slowdown. Fewer deployments could eventually reduce new workloads to secure. But today's security burden comes from the AI already being deployed, including autonomous agents that can make mistakes at machine speed. That makes CrowdStrike and Palo Alto a different kind of AI trade: less dependent on training the next giant model and more dependent on enterprises being nervous about what current models can already do.

articles.title: We don’t need AI regulation — leave safety to us, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says
articles.summary: AI isn't some new form of "alien mind," according to Jensen Huang. It's just hardware and software, so safety can be engineered by each AI product maker.
articles.body:
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang made his position on the dangers AI poses very clear while speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference on Tuesday. To him, AI isn't some new form of "alien mind," as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. It's just hardware and software, he says, built by humans. That means, in his view, it can be controlled by humans and existing laws.

"Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one," he said. "We're developing software after all. We're developing computing systems after all. It's a complicated computing system, but it's ultimately a computing system."

Therefore, there's no need for new laws or regulations to govern it, he argues. In fact, Huang sees little need for new laws at all. The free market, he argues, will be enough to pressure companies not to release unsafe products.

"If we're not confident about the safety of the products, like all companies, like you and I, all the companies here, if you build a product or a service, and you're not confident in its functionality, capability, or safety, then don't release it. And so that's a very obvious thing to do," he said.

He continued: "You pace yourself until you are confident you're releasing something that the market would appreciate. The market forces are already there. We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations. We just need companies to decide that when [to] run as fast as they can. I think innovation, speed, and safe products … it's a false choice. You could definitely have both at the same time. So run as fast as you can. But if you feel at any given point in time the company's out of control, or the product's not going to be safe, you know, take a pause and make sure you get it right."

In some ways, this is a comforting thought. If anyone in the world knows AI, it is Nvidia's founder, who's been building the hardware brains of AI since well before ChatGPT existed and now runs a company that also makes open source models, agents, harnesses, and sandboxes.

Then again, if we're being cynical, his point of view is also unsurprising for someone who's had his bread so well buttered by the AI boom . Why would he want regulation to come along and add in a layer of hinderance that could slow down Nvidia's quest to sell ever more AI systems and software? As he also said in the interview: "I'm more ambitious than ever. As a result of our ambition, and with the product productivity boost that we get from AI, the sky's the limit for us. The sky's the limit for our company. The sky's the limit for every industry, for every single country."

articles.title: SK Hynix Strikes Labor Union Deal to Pay Half of Bonuses in Cash
articles.summary: SK Hynix Inc. has struck an agreement with its union to pay out half of all profit-sharing bonuses in cash, resolving a dispute that threatened to disrupt pr...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SK Hynix Inc. has struck an agreement with its union to pay out half of all profit-sharing bonuses in cash, resolving a dispute that threatened to disrupt production at the world's second-biggest memory chipmaker.

About 57% of the labor group approved a revised wage and collective bargaining agreement, SK Hynix said in a statement Wednesday. In the latest pact, 50% of profit-sharing bonuses will be paid out in cash and half in company shares, replacing a previously proposed 40-60 cash-stock split. The company's shares climbed more than 2% in Seoul.

The agreement resolves tensions at a company that supplies the high-bandwidth memory Nvidia Corp. and other chipmakers need for accelerators fundamental to AI development. The ratification follows about two weeks of re-negotiations after union members rejected an initial, tentative agreement in August, with 50.08% voting against the deal.

A key sticking point had been management's proposal to shift a substantial portion of profit-sharing bonuses from cash to shares, including restricted stock that employees wouldn't have been able to sell immediately. The union initially opposed the proposal, arguing that it would undermine a profit-sharing framework agreed upon last year.

Under that framework, SK Hynix agreed to remove a ceiling on its profit-sharing bonus and allocate 10% of annual operating profits to employees for 10 years. The size and structure of such bonuses have become a closely watched issue not only for SK Hynix and its staff, but also across South Korea as the booming semiconductor sector generates record profits.

The two sides had also agreed that employees would temporarily defer 3% of salaries if SK Hynix posts a loss, with full pay restored once business rebounds.

articles.title: Zuckerberg Has an AI Empire to Build. Meet the Adviser Who Handles the Details
articles.summary: At a Meta Platforms Inc. board retreat last December, Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg asked Dina Powell McCormick to take a walk with him around his...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- At a Meta Platforms Inc. board retreat last December, Chief Executive Officer Mark Zuckerberg asked Dina Powell McCormick to take a walk with him around his sprawling Kauai compound, known as Koolau Ranch.

Zuckerberg told Powell McCormick, a former Trump administration official and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. executive who'd joined the board eight months prior, that the $1.7 trillion company was banking its future on artificial intelligence. To do that, Meta would need to raise a tremendous amount of outside capital. And Zuckerberg would need a right-hand adviser with the robust connections and political capital required to smooth the way with both financial institutions and governments.

"It became clear to me that she could play a bigger role in Meta's next chapter," Zuckerberg recalls. He asked her to trade the board seat for a key internal role. Zuckerberg told her it would be the most important job she'd ever have.

A well-connected power player in both Washington and on Wall Street, Powell McCormick has built relationships with a shocking breadth of people including former US Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, BlackRock Inc. CEO Larry Fink and pop star Katy Perry, and has had plenty of big jobs. But about a week after Zuckerberg's pitch, she resigned from the board. In January, she became president, vice chairman and co-leader of Meta Compute, its effort to build and monetize the infrastructure fueling the AI revolution.

Nine months in, Powell McCormick's remit extends far beyond helping to hash out deals for Meta Compute. Interviews with more than a dozen Meta insiders, outside executives and government officials and Powell McCormick herself show she's an executive trusted by Zuckerberg and his top deputies to tackle the company's thorniest problems – including countering the backlash to AI and weighing in on major legal and reputational fights, like Meta's recent settlement of up to $18 billion with state attorneys general over children's safety on Instagram and Facebook.

Powell McCormick has appeared for Meta at Davos, traveled with President Donald Trump and an entourage of Silicon Valley's most famous to China and met with King Charles III, freeing Zuckerberg to spend his time in Menlo Park with the engineers and researchers rushing to build Meta's next generation of models. While Zuckerberg, 42, is the cerebral engineering leader obsessed with improving Meta's products for the AI race, Powell McCormick, 53, has her pulse on the world outside of Silicon Valley, and can be Meta's bridge to opportunities and fixer of challenges.
authors: Riley Griffin and Alexandra S. Levine

articles.title: Amazon launches Alexa+ in India with Hindi support
articles.summary: Amazon is letting all customers use Alexa+ assistant in early access period.
articles.body:
Amazon today announced that its Alexa+ conversational assistant is available in India with Hindi support. The new assistant can hold conversations for longer and maintain context while doing so.

The feature is available to all customers in the country in Early Access in Hindi and English. After the early testing period, the company will make the assistant free for Prime customers. For non-Prime customers, the price will be ₹2,000 per month ($20.85).

The company said that the new Alexa has a more expressive voice and can handle complex multi-step tasks, including ordering groceries from Amazon’s quick commerce service Amazon Now and turning on/off smart home devices. Users can switch between English and Hindi mid-sentence.

Amazon added that Alexa+ is integrated with India-based services such as food delivery service Swiggy, Zomato’s ticket booking platform District, travel websites like TripAdvisor and MakeMyTrip, and restaurant reservation app EazyDiner. The upgraded assistant is also integrated with music streaming services such as Amazon Music and JioSaavn.

In June, TechCrunch reported that the company had invited users to enroll in a testing program for Alexa+, through which they could have conversations with the assistant in Hindi. After that, the company also started testing an English version of Alexa+ .

Amazon launched Alexa in India in English in 2017 and added Hindi support in 2019. The country has more than 600 million Hindi speakers, and Amazon is trying to tap into that market with its smart devices and new features. The company didn’t give absolute numbers, but said that its smart home devices have grown by 20% from last year.

Amazon initially announced GenAI-powered Alexa+ in 2025 and made it available to all U.S.-based users in 2026 . This year, the company has also launched its new assistant in markets such as the U.K., Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Italy, and Germany with local language context.

articles.title: Trump's AI race with China could become the biggest mistake of our time
articles.summary: AI leaders like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk urge slowing development, but Trump insists America can't pause with China closing in.
articles.body: In less than two weeks, President Donald Trump will welcome Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington. Trump says AI will be a major topic of their September 24 talks and insists America must stay ahead of China. But the race has acquired a second, more dangerous dimension: some of the people building the world’s most powerful AI systems now warn they are advancing faster than humans can safely control them. Jacob Coxon, a researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, resigned from Anthropic last week with a warning: Competition among frontier labs is driving ever more powerful systems forward before researchers know how to keep them reliably under human control. Coxon told WIRED that colleagues described the next year or two as "crunch time for humanity." Days later, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei went further. In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," he argued the industry must deliberately slow how fast it increases model capabilities, so safeguards can catch up. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote, proposing independent evaluators embedded inside frontier labs, coordinated safety standards among democratic nations and eventually international arrangements covering the most dangerous capabilities. He did not call for halting AI development. What began as an Anthropic warning quickly became a rare convergence among rivals. OpenAI’s Sam Altman endorsed Amodei’s call for independent evaluators. Elon Musk responded simply, "Dario is right." Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis backed the same direction, while Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that superintelligence that does not help humanity and does not remain under human control is not worth pursuing. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST None of this proves AI is about to destroy humanity, and some of the alarm deserves skepticism. Anthropic is reportedly preparing an IPO that could value the company at nearly $2 trillion. That raises a fair question: Is some of this rhetoric also advertising the extraordinary power, and therefore potential value, of its technology? Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has accused parts of the industry of stoking cybersecurity fears while preparing products to address them. The incentives deserve scrutiny. But Altman’s decision to delay OpenAI’s IPO until 2027 over safety concerns cuts against the claim that this is merely financial theater. The first AI Cold War question was who would build the most powerful systems. The harder question is whether either side can remain in control of what it builds. But America cannot consider these warnings in a vacuum. China changes the calculation. In earlier Fox News columns, I have warned against regulating America into technological defeat, copying Beijing’s surveillance model or treating this as merely a race between chatbots. As I argue in my book, "The New AI Cold War," the competition spans chips, energy, data centers, cyber operations, military power, scientific discovery and global influence. TRUMP SAYS CHINESE PRESIDENT XI JINPING WILL VISIT US ON SEPT 24 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent captured the strategic bind bluntly: "We can’t pause. You can’t, because the Chinese won’t pause." Trump has now stated the competing imperative just as plainly. Asked Sunday whether AI development should slow, Trump dismissed the warnings as exaggerated, saying unnamed critics were hyping things that won’t happen. "We’re leading China in AI," he said. "Whoever wins AI wins." He said Washington could still add guardrails. Bessent’s concern is understandable; the administration is pursuing both speed and safeguards. Trump’s Genesis Mission links federal scientific data and supercomputing to AI research across more than 15 agencies. His June national security directive accelerates AI adoption while requiring systems to remain "robust, steerable, controllable" and subject to human accountability. A separate executive order provides for voluntary pre-release federal cybersecurity evaluation of frontier models. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL Congress still lacks a comprehensive statutory framework, but the disagreement has become more explicit. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., rejected an emergency moratorium, warning that if lawmakers rush to regulate, China will close the gap. Former White House AI advisor David Sacks made the sharper free-market argument: Laboratories that want to slow down can do so themselves. They should not use Washington to force smaller competitors to apply the same brakes. REP. TED LIEU: AI IS ALREADY TOO POWERFUL. WE NEED A KILL SWITCH BEFORE DISASTER STRIKES Other lawmakers are proposing approaches ranging from bans on superintelligence to narrower requirements that developers test and disclose catastrophic risks. Washington broadly agrees that something consequential is happening. It does not agree on what to do about it. Then there is China. On Sept. 8, U.S. cyber and law enforcement officials accused Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of distilling American AI technology "at an industrial scale." Beijing rejected the accusations and called distillation a common industry technique. That dispute exposes the danger of unilateral American restraint. Washington can regulate American laboratories; it cannot order Beijing to accept identical limits. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Beijing made that point explicit this week. Responding Monday to Amodei’s proposal, China’s Foreign Ministry denounced what it called fearmongering and warned that confrontation would disrupt global AI governance. Washington wants China to cooperate on slowing the most dangerous capabilities while restricting Beijing’s access to the chips and model capabilities that could close the gap. Amodei himself recognizes this: Slowing democratic AI development beyond the American lead could let Chinese Communist Party-linked projects move ahead and create new dangers. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY Yet an unrestricted race creates a different danger. Every laboratory races because its rivals race. Every nation accelerates because it fears falling behind. That is the classic security dilemma I have warned about in "The New AI Cold War." Actions one side takes to increase its security can drive the other side to accelerate, leaving both less secure. The Sept. 24 summit arrives at that moment. Reuters reported preparations for U.S.-China AI safety discussions covering AI-directed cyberattacks and incident information-sharing, though the White House said no separate meeting had been formally scheduled. The choices range from racing ahead to stopping outright. Between them lie more practical options: safety requirements triggered by dangerous capabilities, independent evaluations, and narrow agreements governing catastrophic uses. And any agreement faces a brutal problem: verification. Nuclear arms control dealt with warheads, missiles and enrichment plants that leave physical signatures; frontier AI resides largely in software, model weights and computing infrastructure. Amodei acknowledges that limited agreements on clearly dangerous applications may be more realistic than a comprehensive pause, while more ambitious restrictions become progressively harder to verify. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That is the defining paradox of the new AI Cold War. America cannot afford to let China dominate artificial intelligence, but competition does not make technological risk disappear. Trump says whoever wins AI wins. Amodei, Altman, Musk and other industry leaders warn that winning the race will mean little if the winner cannot control what it builds. Beijing, meanwhile, says it supports AI cooperation while rejecting an American strategy designed to preserve the U.S. technological advantage. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That leaves Trump and Xi with a harder problem than simply deciding who gets there first. The first AI Cold War question was who would build the most powerful systems. The harder question is whether either side can remain in control of what it builds. With Xi coming to Washington on Sept. 24, that is no longer merely an engineering problem. It is a problem of national strategy. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ROBERT MAGINNIS

articles.title: In 2018, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said that Facebook is the new cigarette, 8 years later he has similar warning for ChatGPT and Claude-makers; says: Do not ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Eight years after Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff called Facebook “the new cigarettes”, he is raising a similar concern about the fast-growing AI industry.
articles.body: Eight years after Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff called Facebook “the new cigarettes”, he is raising a similar concern about the fast-growing AI industry, including companies behind tools such as ChatGPT and Claude. During the company’s annual summit, Marc Benioff has warned that the technology could repeat some of the problems created by social media if companies do not take responsibility for its wider impact. His comments come as the debate around AI safety, ChatGPT, Claude and responsible AI development grows. Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for frontier AI labs to slow the pace of development so safety measures can keep up.Marc Benioff warns AI companies not to repeat social media mistakesMarc Benioff said AI companies need to avoid problems that social media platforms face. “A lot of companies got hurt, a lot of individuals got hurt through social media,” Benioff told Jim Cramer in a Mad Money interview during Salesforce's Dreamforce event in San Francisco. “We don’t want that to happen in AI.”Benioff's comments come as Salesforce continues to work with companies developing generative AI. Last month, Salesforce announced Claudeforce, which includes a plugin that allows customers to use Anthropic's Claude with data stored in Salesforce. The tool can also perform tasks such as writing emails and updating records.Anthropic CEO attends Dreamforce keynoteAnthropic CEO Dario Amodei also appeared on stage during Benioff's Dreamforce keynote on Tuesday. “I think that’s the way to lead the industry forward, to set an example, to say that everyone can always be better,” Amodei said.Notably, Benioff did not call for AI development to be slowed or directly criticised individual AI companies. Instead, he said companies developing the technology have a responsibility to consider its wider effects. “We want AI to take care of these things and be held responsible, and take care of these actions and be ethical,” Benioff said. “The heart of ethics is responsibility.”He added:“We really look at a light on our brethren here in San Francisco and all over the world and say, ‘We want you to be ethical in your actions and how you take care of your communities and the world,’ because this technology is very powerful.”Get the latest technology news and updates.
